title: Merit is no merit (section 19)
hook: merit is called merit because it is no fixed thing

segments.voice: Yesterday: past, present and future mind. None of them can be caught and held. Your line: can't be grasped. When a worry gripped you, did the line loosen it? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

A paper punch card sits in a wallet, nine holes punched, one to go. A child's chore chart on the fridge is crowded with gold stars. An app counts your steps and throws confetti when you reach the goal. We are creatures who like a tally. There is a pleasure in watching the good add up. Buddhist life has its own word for the good that adds up, and it's an important one: merit. Section nineteen of the Diamond Sutra picks that word up, turns it over once, and sets it down differently. Today: merit is no merit.
screen: `A PUNCH CARD, A STAR CHART.` → `WE LIKE A TALLY.` → `THE WORD MERIT.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Merit, in Sanskrit punya, in Pali puñña, is the good that comes from good deeds: giving, keeping precepts, honoring teachers, meditating. In Buddhist communities it's a real and living idea. People give food to monks, light lamps, sponsor a reading, and speak of the merit of it, and sometimes share that merit with those who have died. The Diamond Sutra doesn't throw any of that away. It comes back to merit again and again. Second, the question. The Buddha asks Subhuti once more about a gift on a staggering scale: someone fills a whole vast world system with the seven precious things and gives it all away. Would that person gain much merit from it? Very much, Subhuti says. Third, the turn. And here's the whole of section nineteen's surprise, in one sentence. If merit were a real, solid thing, the Buddha says, the Tathagata would not call it much merit. It's because merit is no fixed thing that he calls it much. Read that slowly. The merit isn't denied. The size of it isn't denied. What's taken away is the idea that it's a thing you can stack, own, and carry around in a pocket. Fourth, the lightness. Some readers hear in this a relief. If merit were a pile, you'd have to guard it, compare it, worry about losing it. Because it's so-called merit, a name for the way good spreads out, there is nothing to guard. You can do good and let it go, the way a river doesn't keep the water it passes on. The good is still good. It just isn't yours to count.
screen: `PUNYA: THE GOOD THAT GROWS.` · `A WORLD OF TREASURE GIVEN.` · `NO FIXED THING, SO MUCH.` · `NOTHING TO GUARD.` · then, large: `SO-CALLED MERIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: do good lightly. This time, start from the other side of the ledger. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a kindness someone did for you that you never paid back: a ride, a meal, a word at the right moment, a debt nobody ever mentioned. Notice the pull to balance it, to owe, to even things up. No need to fight that pull. Just see it. Then let the kindness stay unbalanced, a gift that was never a transaction. Breathe in, receiving it. Breathe out, letting it pass on through you, toward someone you haven't met yet. No tally on either side. The bell holds the time.
Merit is no merit. Section nineteen says the Tathagata calls merit much precisely because it is no fixed thing. Today's word.
Your line: so-called merit. Today, do one good thing and tell no one, not even yourself later. Let it go uncounted. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: In Buddhist communities people make merit by giving to monks and nuns, keeping precepts and supporting teaching, and some dedicate or share that merit with others; Mahayana teachers read section 19 as a reminder not to cling to merit as a possession.

fork.setup: you're Subhuti. someone gives away a whole world filled with seven treasures. the Buddha asks: much merit? what do you say?
options: only if they tell no one
fork.reveal: Subhuti says very much, and the Buddha explains: it's called much because merit is no fixed thing.

original.note: Sanskrit: merit, the good that comes from good deeds; Pali puñña.

trapdoor: what you thought: merit is a score you build up.
what it means: merit is real and great, but it's no fixed thing you can own.
what a scholar hears: the sutra's pattern, x is not x, therefore called x, applied to punya itself.

notes: Section 19 paraphrased, not quoted (Max Müller's wording unverified): check the world-system filled with the seven treasures, Subhuti's 'very much', and 'if merit were a real thing the Tathagata would not call it much'.
The description of merit-making (food to monks, lamps, sponsoring readings, sharing merit with the dead) is general Buddhist practice, not from section 19; confirm it is fair across schools.
The river image is the writer's, not the sutra's.
